It would be proven wrong by a run or test that writes `empty_trace`, `malformed_answer` or `entry_mismatch` as a path's `break_reason`.
- pydantic serialises `BreakReason` as a bare JSON string, not as `"BreakReason.text_mismatch"` or an object. It would be proven wrong if `model_dump(mode="json")` returns anything other than a `str` equal to the member value.
- Changing any member's spelling changes the re-ask cache key. It would be proven wrong if two keys built with different `break_reason` strings hash the same.

### How we would find out cheaply
1. Check the registry (about 5 seconds): run `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://pypi.org/pypi/break-reason/json`. Getting `200` instead of `404` falsifies assumption 1. Then run `rg -n 'import break_reason|from break_reason' plugins/multiplai-dev/lib/code_facts`. Any hit falsifies assumption 2.
2. Run this pydantic check from the code_facts dir with `uv run python -I -c '…'`:
   ```python
   from typing import Literal; from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict
   BR = Literal["path_outside_root","missing_file","line_out_of_range","text_mismatch","base_side_citation","entry_mismatch","unconnected_hop","repeated_hop","malformed_answer","empty_trace","hop_limit"]
   class P(BaseModel): model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid"); break_reason: BR | None = None
   print(P(break_reason="text_mismatch").model_dump(mode="json"), P.model_json_schema()["properties"]["break_reason"])
   P(break_reason="route")  # expect ValidationError
   ```
   Assumption 5 is falsified if the dump isn't `{'break_reason': 'text_mismatch'}`, or if `"route"` is accepted. If the printed enum includes `empty_trace`, `malformed_answer` and `entry_mismatch`, the schema advertises values that can never be published.
3. Once `paths.py` exists, add one test. Run `map_paths` with a `FakeCall` that returns zero hops twice, then a 21-hop valid answer for a second entry. Assert three things: the first entry appears only in `dropped` with `("trace","empty_trace")`; the second has `stops_at == 20` and `break_reason == "hop_limit"` and the fake was called exactly once for it; and no written path's `break_reason` is outside the eight values in assumption 4. Then build two re-ask keys that differ only in `break_reason` and assert their digests differ (assumption 6).

Neither PyPI nor npm has a package called "broken-at". It looks like the design's internal `broken_at` field. Next I'm checking the walkthrough's existing gate to compare its meaning.## broken-at

### What it is
`broken-at` is not a third-party package. Nobody maintains it as a library, it has no docs, changelog or issue tracker, and it is not installable. Both `https://pypi.org/pypi/broken-at/json` and `https://pypi.org/pypi/broken_at/json` return HTTP 404, and so does `https://registry.npmjs.org/broken-at`. The dependency scanner picked up the field name **`broken_at`** from design.md § Decisions. That field belongs to the new, project-owned `GateOutcome` returned by `code_facts.gate.check_trace` (D9). It also appears in the re-ask cache key (D7: "the trace key | first-answer digest | `broken_at` | `break_reason`"). Its job in this change is to hold the 1-based index of the first hop that fails the trace gate. That index produces the published `stops_at` (`broken_at - 1`, or 20 for the hop limit) and decides whether to re-ask or drop. The closest code already in the repo is `trace_gate` in `skills/codebase-walkthrough/scripts/walkthrough_pipeline/gates.py:188-215` and how `stages/trace.py:97-114` uses it. That older code uses a **different** convention, and this section is mostly about that mismatch. Action: don't add anything to `pyproject.toml`, and treat this entry as a false positive from the scanner.

### The contract we rely on
Nothing here is external. The contract is the one the design defines for itself, plus the existing walkthrough gate it replaces.

- New (design D9), quoted verbatim: `GateOutcome(accepted: list[Hop], broken_at: int | None, reason: BreakReason | None, detail: str)` returned by `check_trace(hops, *, entry, edges, places, resolve, root) -> GateOutcome`.
  - `broken_at` is the 1-based index of the first broken hop, or `None` if every hop passed.
  - `malformed_answer` and `empty_trace` both give `broken_at=1`.
  - More than 20 hops gives `broken_at=21, reason="hop_limit"` with no re-ask. Exactly 20 hops is not a cut.
  - Published `stops_at = broken_at - 1`, or `20` for `hop_limit`. `stops_at` and `break_reason` must both be null or both be set, with `1 ≤ stops_at ≤ len(hops)`.
  - After the single re-ask, if the result still has `broken_at == 1`, the entry is dropped at stage `trace` with reason `malformed_trace`, `empty_trace` or `cut_at_entry`.
- Existing (walkthrough), verbatim: `def trace_gate(repos: dict[str, RepoInfo], seed: SymbolEntry | Reference, hops: list[Hop], places: list[tuple[str, int]]) -> tuple[int, str]:`, docstring `"(number of good hops from the start, reason for the first bad one or "")."`
  - It returns a **count of good hops**, not a 1-based index: `0, "no hops"` for an empty list, `k, …` when hop k+1 fails, `len(hops), ""` when all pass.
  - `walkthrough_pipeline/models.py:153` says `stops_at: int | None = None   # 1-based hop index the trace stops at, when it broke`. But `trace.py:114` stores `stops_at=good`, which is the count of kept hops. The comment and the code disagree.

### Edge cases & failure modes
- **Empty input (zero hops).** The old gate returns `(0, "no hops")`, and `trace.py` still writes a `Scenario` with `hops=[]` and `stops_at=0`. The design instead says `broken_at=1`, `empty_trace`, one re-ask, then a drop. So the same empty answer gives a 0-hop path in the walkthrough and no path at all in `paths.json`. Anything comparing the two will disagree.
- **Agent failure.** On a cached `{"error": …}`, the walkthrough produces `stops_at=0, break_reason="the trace agent failed"`. `0` breaks the new contract's `1 ≤ stops_at` invariant. Any code that copies the walkthrough's sentinel will fail the `_Strict` validator.
- **Malformed input / hop 1 not at the entry.** The old gate returns `0` both for a hop-1 citation failure and for "hop 1 is not the seed". The new gate gives `broken_at=1` with distinct reasons (`entry_mismatch` vs `text_mismatch` …). The old code produces one value, `0`, for four different causes, so tests ported from `test_gates.py` will assert the wrong number. That file's `test_trace_gate_stops_at_a_broken_hop` and `test_stages.py:58` (`webhook["stops_at"] == 2 and len(webhook["hops"]) == 2`) both use the count meaning.
- **Off-by-one between the specs.** The same third-hop failure gives three numbers: the old gate returns `2`, the new `broken_at` is `3`, and the published `stops_at` is `2`. The trace-gate spec scenarios ("breaks at hop 3 → stops_at 3") use the index meaning. The output contract ("third hop fails → `stops_at: 2`") uses the count meaning. D9 settles this, but only if every scenario is rewritten as `broken_at == n` plus `stops_at == n-1`.
- **Oversized input.** The old gate has no hop limit and checks every hop, however many there are. The new limit of 20 gives `broken_at=21`, so `broken_at` can be bigger than `len(accepted)+1` would suggest for a normal break, and `stops_at=20` has no `+1` relationship to it. Code that computes `stops_at = broken_at - 1` everywhere publishes 20 by luck. Code that computes `len(hops) - 1` does not.
- **Repeated use (re-ask).** The walkthrough keeps whichever of the first answer and the re-ask has more good hops (`if g2 > good or …`). The design keeps the **re-answer's** prefix even when it is shorter. So a re-ask can shorten a path that the old pipeline would have kept longer. The design also feeds `broken_at` into the re-ask cache key. A non-deterministic gate input, such as a file change between runs, would therefore produce a different key and a fresh paid call instead of a cache hit.
- **Concurrent use.** `check_trace` is designed to be pure and synchronous, with no shared state, so `broken_at` itself has no thread-safety concerns. The walkthrough's `ask` writes into a shared `state.trace_answers` dict from concurrent tasks. That is safe only because asyncio runs on one thread. The design replaces it with one file per key in `DirAnswers`.
- **Offline / unavailable / unauthenticated.** Not applicable as a dependency: `broken_at` is a local integer, and no network or auth is involved. The gate reads files with `git show <sha>:<rel>`. If git is missing or the sha can't be reached, the result is `missing_file` (rule 2) at that hop, not an exception. Unknown: whether `resolve`/`git show` failures raise or return None in the new gate — check by calling `check_trace` with a resolver pointing at a bogus sha and seeing whether you get an exception or `broken_at=1, reason="missing_file"`.

### Assumptions we are making
- No package called `broken-at`/`broken_at` needs installing. Proven wrong if any import or `uv lock` step fails resolving that name.
- `broken_at` is always `None` or an integer ≥ 1. It is never `0`, and `0` never appears in `paths.json` `stops_at`. Proven wrong by a fixture with an empty or failed trace that writes `stops_at: 0`.
- For every written path, `stops_at == broken_at - 1` when `reason != "hop_limit"`, and `stops_at == 20` when it is. Proven wrong by any written path where `len(hops) != stops_at`.
- A trace that has `broken_at == 1` after the re-ask never produces a path. It always produces exactly one `DropRecord` at stage `trace`. Proven wrong if kept + drops ≠ E in the accounting test.
- Exactly 20 valid hops gives `broken_at is None`, and 21 gives `broken_at == 21` with exactly one `CallFn` call (no re-ask). Proven wrong by the fake `CallFn` recording 2 calls for the 21-hop case.
- No code in `code_facts/` imports or copies `walkthrough_pipeline.gates.trace_gate`'s count-based return. Proven wrong by the AST guard test finding the import, or by a `stops_at=good` pattern in the new code.
- Ported walkthrough tests are rewritten from count meaning to index meaning. Proven wrong if a ported test asserts `broken_at == 2` for a hop-3 failure.

### How we would find out cheaply
1. Confirm it is not a package (already done; repeat in CI if you like):
   `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://pypi.org/pypi/broken-at/json` gives `404`. A `200` would falsify "no package needed".
2. Pin the old convention so nobody copies it by accident. From `skills/codebase-walkthrough/scripts`, run:
   ```python
   from walkthrough_pipeline.gates import trace_gate
   print(trace_gate({}, seed, [], []))          # expect (0, 'no hops')  -> count meaning, not index
   ```
   Any result other than `(0, …)` means the walkthrough has already changed convention.
3. A five-case table test against the new gate, once `gate.py` exists, with a git-init fixture and a prefix resolver:
   ```python
   cases = {"empty": ([], 1, "empty_trace"),
            "hop3_bad": (h[:2] + [bad] , 3, "text_mismatch"),
            "twenty": (valid20, None, None),
            "twentyone": (valid21, 21, "hop_limit"),
            "hop1_wrong_file": ([elsewhere], 1, "entry_mismatch")}
   for name, (hops, b, r) in cases.items():
       o = check_trace(hops, entry=e, edges=(), places=(), resolve=res, root=root)
       assert (o.broken_at, o.reason) == (b, r), name
   ```
   Then run `map_paths` with a `FakeCall` returning these answers. Assert:
   - `stops_at ∈ {2, None, None, 20}` for the surviving cases, and `empty`/`hop1_wrong_file` show up only in `dropped` with stage `trace`;
   - `FakeCall.calls` is 2 for `empty`/`hop3_bad`/`hop1_wrong_file` and 1 for `twenty`/`twentyone`.

   Any mismatch falsifies the matching assumption above.
4. `rg -n 'stops_at\s*=\s*good|trace_gate' plugins/multiplai-dev/lib/code_facts` should print nothing. Any hit falsifies the no-copy assumption.

## cache-dir

### What it is
`cache-dir` is not a third-party package. `https://pypi.org/pypi/cache-dir/json` returns HTTP 404, and nothing needs adding to `pyproject.toml`. The scanner picked up the `cache_dir: Path | None` keyword of `map_paths` (D2/D7). What the change actually relies on is a new in-house class, `DirAnswers(MutableMapping[str, dict])`. It stores one JSON file per answer key, written with `tempfile` plus `os.replace`, and it is handed to the existing `code_facts.explore.ask` / `run_tasks` as their `answers` mapping. The behaviour that matters comes from three places:
- the Python 3.12+ standard library (`os.replace`, `tempfile.mkstemp`, `hashlib.sha256`, `json`, `collections.abc.MutableMapping`), maintained by CPython;
- the `ask` / `run_tasks` / `gate_answers` code in `plugins/multiplai-dev/lib/code_facts/code_facts/explore.py`, maintained by this repo;
- the repo's own atomic-write convention (`build_pipeline/state.py:303-315`).

This section covers what the design gets from that combination: answers that survive a restart, and no repeated paid work.

### The contract we rely on
From `code_facts/explore.py`, quoted verbatim:

```python
async def ask(key: str, prompt: str, call: CallFn, answers: dict[str, dict], *,
              call_kwargs: dict[str, Any], errors: list[str],
              recoverable: tuple[type[BaseException], ...] = (Exception,),
              fatal: tuple[type[BaseException], ...] = (),
              progress: Callable[[str], None] | None = None) -> None:
    try:
        out = await call(prompt, ExploreOutput, budget_label=f"explore:{key.split(':')[0]}", **call_kwargs)
        answers[key] = out.model_dump()
    except fatal:
        raise
    except recoverable as e:
        ...
        answers[key] = {"error": first}
        errors.append(f"explore {key}: {first}")
    if progress:
        progress(f"  explore {key}: {len(answers[key].get('facts', []))} facts")

async def run_tasks(tasks: list[tuple[str, str]], call: CallFn, answers: dict[str, dict], *,
                    concurrency: int, **ask_kwargs: Any) -> None:
    await bounded([t for t in tasks if t[0] not in answers], one, concurrency)
```

`gate_answers(answers, keep, ...)` iterates `answers.items()` and skips any value that contains the key `"error"`.

From the standard library:
- `os.replace(src, dst)`: "If successful, the renaming will be an atomic operation (this is a POSIX requirement)." It "may fail if src and dst are on different filesystems."
- `tempfile.mkstemp(suffix=None, prefix=None, dir=None, text=False)`: the file is "readable and writable only by the creating user ID".
- `collections.abc.MutableMapping`: the abstract methods are `__getitem__`, `__setitem__`, `__delitem__`, `__iter__` and `__len__`. The mixin `__contains__` is `try: self[key] except KeyError: return False`.

What D7 promises:
- the file is `cache_dir/<sha256(key)>.json`;
- each write uses a tempfile in the same directory, then `os.replace`;
- with `cache_dir=None` a plain `dict` is used and nothing touches disk.

### Edge cases & failure modes
Everything below comes from reading `explore.py` and the Python documentation, not from running anything. That is why some bullets say "the code shows" and others are marked Unknown.

- **Empty or degenerate input: `Path("")` means the working directory.** `Path("")` becomes `PosixPath('.')`, so `cache_dir=Path("")` would write 64-hex-character `.json` files into whatever directory the process is running in, with no error. A `cache_dir` that doesn't exist only works if `DirAnswers` calls `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)`. A `cache_dir` that is a regular file raises `FileExistsError` from `mkdir`, or `NotADirectoryError` on the first write. An empty directory works: every key misses and every task is asked.
- **Empty or degenerate input: an empty or truncated answer file aborts the whole run.** `run_tasks` checks `t[0] not in answers` once, before any task starts. The mixin `__contains__` calls `__getitem__` and catches only `KeyError`. A zero-byte file therefore makes `json.loads` raise `json.JSONDecodeError` (a `ValueError`) out of the `in` test, and the run stops before any call is made. The same thing happens for any file the user edited by hand. `DirAnswers.__getitem__` has to turn unreadable files into `KeyError`, or delete them.
- **Malformed or unexpected-format input: `ask` hard-codes the explore schema.** It calls `call(prompt, ExploreOutput, ...)` and stores `out.model_dump()`. Reusing `ask` "unchanged" (D7) for `TraceAnswer` or `FallbackAnswer` would send the wrong schema to the model. Also, if `CallFn` returns a `dict` or `str` (which D5 allows), `out.model_dump()` raises `AttributeError`:
  - under `ask`'s own default `recoverable=(Exception,)`, that error is silently stored as `{"error": "'dict' object has no attribute 'model_dump'"}`;
  - under D6's `recoverable=()`, it propagates. (`except ():` catches nothing.)

  `ask` needs a `schema` parameter and normalisation, or a sibling function.
- **Malformed or unexpected-format input: `budget_label` collides.** `ask` always passes `budget_label=` and also spreads `**call_kwargs`. If `call_kwargs` contains `budget_label` (D2 gives it as an example), Python raises `TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'budget_label'` before the call runs. Under `recoverable=(Exception,)`, every key would then be stored as an error. Separately, the label is built from `key.split(':')[0]`. That gives `explore:fallback` for fallback keys and `explore:<64-hex>` for a bare-digest trace key, so budget reports would show one label per entry instead of one per stage.
- **Malformed or unexpected-format input: keys are hashed, and the original key is lost.** The filename is `sha256(key)`, so `__iter__` over the directory can only return hashes unless each file also stores its original key. `gate_answers` iterates `answers.items()`, and directory listing order is filesystem-dependent. A shared `cache_dir` would also return other commits' answers. To keep D7's "rebuilt in canonical order" true, the output has to be rebuilt by looking up the keys this run computes, never by iterating the directory.
- **Malformed or unexpected-format input: some values fail canonical JSON.** `json.dumps(sort_keys=True)` sorts dict keys but not lists. It turns tuples into lists, raises `TypeError` on `Path`, `set` and plain `Enum`, and by default writes `NaN`, which is not valid JSON. `ask` stores `model_dump()` in Python mode, not `mode="json"`, so any non-JSON field type inside an answer fails only when the file is written, after the call has been paid for.
- **Oversized input: hashing removes the filename limit, but nothing limits size or count.** Every filename is 69 characters (`64 + ".json"`), whatever the key's length, so `NAME_MAX` (255) is never hit. There is no limit on answer size and no eviction. Each run adds up to `2 × trace_limit + 1` files (trace, re-ask, fallback) per distinct commit, forever.
- **Oversized input: a full disk loses a paid answer.** `answers[key] = out.model_dump()` runs inside `ask`'s `try`. If `__setitem__` raises `OSError(ENOSPC)`:
  - when `OSError` is recoverable, the `except` branch runs `answers[key] = {"error": ...}`, which raises again and propagates;
  - when it is not recoverable, it propagates directly.

  Either way the answer just paid for is lost, and the next run pays again.
- **Concurrent or repeated use: one process is safe.** `bounded` runs on one event loop thread, and `__setitem__` is synchronous, so writes never interleave. Each write does blocking file I/O on the loop thread. That stalls other coroutines briefly, but they cannot corrupt it.
- **Concurrent or repeated use: two processes on one `cache_dir` pay twice.** Both see a miss, both call, and both `os.replace` onto the same name; the last write wins. Neither file is ever half-written, but both calls are paid. The error purge at the start of a run can also delete an `{"error": …}` file that the other process has just written. There is no locking.
- **Concurrent or repeated use: a kill leaves a temp file behind.** `SIGKILL` between `mkstemp` and `os.replace` skips `finally`. If the temp suffix is `.json`, a glob-based `__len__` or `__iter__` would count it as an answer. Use `prefix="."` and `suffix=".tmp"`, as `epic/store.py:247` does.
- **Concurrent or repeated use: crash durability.** A process kill is safe, because the page cache survives. D7 as written has no `fsync` (`build_pipeline/state.py:310-311` does have one), so after a power loss or OS crash a renamed file can be zero-length on some filesystems. That file then hits the `JSONDecodeError` abort described under empty input.
- **Concurrent or repeated use: file permissions.** Files created by `mkstemp` are mode `0600`, and `os.replace` keeps that mode. Cache files are therefore owner-only, whatever the umask, which matters if the cache is shared across users or CI steps.
- **Offline / unavailable / unauthenticated: a read-only directory fails late.** No network is involved. On a read-only or permission-denied directory, `mkdir(exist_ok=True)` on an existing directory succeeds. The first failure (`PermissionError` or `EROFS`) only comes at the first `__setitem__`, after the first model call has been paid for (see the full-disk bullet).
- **Offline / unavailable / unauthenticated: network and cross-device directories.** Unknown: whether `os.replace` is atomic and immediately visible to a second client when `cache_dir` is on NFS or SMB — check by running the concurrency experiment below with `cache_dir` on such a mount. Putting the tempfile in the same directory avoids `EXDEV` (the cross-device error).

### Assumptions we are making
- `ask` and `run_tasks` can be reused without changes for trace, re-ask and fallback answers. **False as written:** `ask` hard-codes `ExploreOutput` and calls `.model_dump()` on whatever comes back.
- Passing `call_kwargs={"budget_label": ...}` through `ask` reaches `CallFn`. **False as written:** it raises `TypeError` for duplicate keyword arguments.
- A truncated, empty or hand-edited cache file makes that one key miss and get asked again; it does not abort the run.
- `gate_answers`, or whatever rebuilds the output, reads answers by the keys this run computes, so two runs with identical inputs produce byte-identical `paths.json` whatever the directory listing order, and even when other runs' files are in the directory.
- `DirAnswers.__len__` / `__iter__` never count leftover `*.tmp` files.
- After `SIGKILL` at any point during a run, every key whose `os.replace` returned has a file that parses as JSON.
- A write failure (`ENOSPC`, `EROFS`) shows up before the first paid call, because a probe write runs at start-up, and never after the first answer.
- Canonical-JSON keys are stable across processes and Python versions. In particular, no key component is a `Path`, a `set`, an `Enum` or a float.
- With `cache_dir=None`, no file or directory is created anywhere, including the working directory.
- Two concurrent `map_paths` processes on one `cache_dir` never produce a file that fails `json.loads`. (Double spend is accepted.)

### How we would find out cheaply
One script, about 25 lines, run with `uv run python -I probe.py` from `plugins/multiplai-dev/lib/code_facts`:

```python
import asyncio, json, os, tempfile, hashlib
from pathlib import Path
from collections.abc import MutableMapping
from code_facts.explore import ask, run_tasks
class D(MutableMapping):
    def __init__(s, d): s.d = Path(d); s.d.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    def _p(s, k): return s.d / (hashlib.sha256(k.encode()).hexdigest() + ".json")
    def __getitem__(s, k): return json.loads(s._p(k).read_text())   # naive on purpose
    def __setitem__(s, k, v):
        fd, t = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=s.d, prefix=".", suffix=".tmp")
        with os.fdopen(fd, "w") as f: json.dump(v, f)
        os.replace(t, s._p(k))
    def __delitem__(s, k): s._p(k).unlink()
    def __iter__(s): return iter(p.stem for p in s.d.glob("*.json"))
    def __len__(s): return sum(1 for _ in s)
async def call(prompt, schema, **kw): print("schema:", schema.__name__, kw); return {"hops": []}
d = D(tempfile.mkdtemp()); errs = []
asyncio.run(ask("trace:x", "p", call, d, call_kwargs={}, errors=errs)); print(d["trace:x"], errs)        # A1
try: asyncio.run(ask("k", "p", call, d, call_kwargs={"budget_label": "b"}, errors=[]))
except TypeError as e: print("A2 false:", e)
print(d["k"])                                                                                               # A2 (error stored?)
d._p("bad").write_text("")                                                                                  # A3
try: asyncio.run(run_tasks([("bad", "p")], call, d, concurrency=1, call_kwargs={}, errors=[])); print("A3 ok")
except ValueError as e: print("A3 false:", type(e).__name__)
print(oct(d._p("trace:x").stat().st_mode & 0o777), Path(""))                                                # mode, cwd trap
```

How to read the output:
- **A1 (reuse unchanged) is falsified** if it prints `schema: ExploreOutput` and stores `{"error": "'dict' object has no attribute 'model_dump'"}`.
- **A2 (`budget_label` pass-through) is falsified** if the duplicate-keyword `TypeError` appears, either raised or stored under `"k"`.
- **A3 (a corrupt file means a miss) is falsified** if it prints `A3 false: JSONDecodeError`.
- **The mode check** prints `0o600` if the permission behaviour above holds, and `Path("")` prints `.`.

Two follow-ups:
- **Crash and concurrency:** run the same `D` from two processes (`for i in $(seq 200); do python -I w.py & done; wait`), each writing the same key 100 times, then `kill -9` one process part-way through. Then `json.loads` every `*.json` file and count the `*.tmp` files. Any parse failure falsifies the kill-safety and concurrency assumptions. Any `.tmp` file left behind confirms the leftover-temp bullet.
- **Read-only directory:** run `chmod 500 <dir>` before the first `__setitem__`. The assumption that write failures surface before the first paid call is falsified if `call` has already printed before the `PermissionError`.

## changed-lines

### What it is
`changed-lines` is **not a third-party dependency**. The scanner flagged it because of the `changed_lines` keyword in D2's `map_paths` signature. Evidence:
- **PyPI:** `https://pypi.org/pypi/changed-lines/json` returns HTTP 404, so no package by that name exists.
- **npm:** a package called `changed-lines` does exist. It is v1.0.0 by aleclarson, last published 2018-05-21, MIT licensed, and its description is "Compare strings just like `git diff` does". It is a JavaScript string differ and has nothing to do with this Python change.
- **Project code:** no `changed_lines` or `changed-lines` appears anywhere in the installed multiplai plugin tree.
- **`pyproject.toml`:** code-facts declares only `multiplai-core[sdk]` and `pydantic>=2`. The note "0 declared name(s) scanned" means the scan did not read that file's dependency list.

What the change really depends on is a **data contract**: a `Mapping[str, Iterable[int]]` of changed head-side line numbers per snapshot-relative path. The caller (the review / buildme pipelines in PRs 2–4) builds this mapping. The code that produces it today is `review_pipeline/checks.py:diff_hunks`, and similar `@@` parsers live in `review_pipeline/facts.py`, `post.py` and `review_viewer/gitdata.py`. `map_paths` uses the mapping to:
- validate paths and lines;
- seed reachability;
- build cache keys;
- compute coverage, drop paths that cover nothing, and rank the rest.

Nobody maintains it except this project.

### The contract we rely on
The consumer side comes from D2 and D10, verbatim:

```python
changed_lines: Mapping[str, Iterable[int]] | None = None,
scope_paths: Sequence[str] = (),  # fallback scope when changed_lines is None
```

What D10 promises:
- Paths are normalised to POSIX with no leading `./`.
- Absolute or root-escaping paths raise `ValueError`, and so do lines `< 1`. All validation happens before any `CallFn` call.
- A missing file is tolerated.
- `None` means unscoped. `{}` means empty scope, so the fallback is `skipped` with reason `empty_scope` (D5).

The producer that exists today is `review/scripts/review_pipeline/checks.py:94`, verbatim:

```python
def diff_hunks(diff: str) -> dict[str, list[tuple[int, int]]]:
    """New-side line ranges of every hunk, per path (deleted files have none)."""
```
- It returns inclusive `(start, end)` **ranges**, not `Iterable[int]`. Callers must expand each range with `range(s, e + 1)`.
- It matches hunk headers with `_HUNK = re.compile(r"^@@ -\d+(?:,\d+)? \+(\d+)(?:,(\d+))? @@")`.
- It takes the path from `+++ ` lines, strips one `b/` prefix, and maps `/dev/null` to "no path".
- It skips hunks with a new-side count of 0.

No library documentation exists. The contract is only what D2/D10 say and what this function does.

### Edge cases & failure modes
These come from reading `diff_hunks` and D2/D10. None of it has been run yet.

- **Empty or degenerate input:**
  - A diff that only deletes lines (`@@ -20,3 +19,0 @@`) has new-side count 0, so `diff_hunks` emits **nothing** for that file.
  - A deleted file (`+++ /dev/null`) also emits nothing.
  - The surprise: a change made only of deletions gives either `{}` (the fallback is skipped as `empty_scope`, every path has zero coverage and is dropped as `no_changed_line_covered`) or a mapping with that file missing. No error is raised, so `paths.json` comes out empty but valid.
  - Passing `{}` and passing `None` behave in opposite ways. `{}` means scoped with nothing in scope. `None` means unscoped, every entry is traced and `cap: null`.
- **Malformed or unexpected-format input:**
  - **Quoted paths.** git C-quotes paths with spaces or non-ASCII characters (`+++ "b/my file.py"`). `diff_hunks` strips `b/` only from unquoted names, so the key becomes `"b/my file.py"` with the quotes included. D10 accepts it: it is not absolute and does not escape root. A missing file is tolerated, so the change silently covers nothing.
  - **Other prefixes.** `diff.noprefix=true` or `diff.mnemonicPrefix` (`w/`, `i/`, `c/`) leave the prefix in place, with the same silent result.
  - **Wrong element types.** A `str` value passes as `Iterable[int]`, but `"12"` iterates as `"1"`, `"2"`. Unknown: whether D10 rejects that with `ValueError` or crashes on the comparison with a `TypeError` — pass `{"a.py": "12"}` and see what is raised. `True` is an `int` and would be read as line 1.
- **Oversized input:**
  - There is no limit on paths or line counts. A whole-file rewrite of a 50k-line generated file turns into 50k ints. These are sorted into **every** trace cache key and rendered as "changed ranges" in every `trace_entry` prompt, which makes the prompts bigger and gives no truncation warning.
  - Unknown: does D7's "sorted changed ranges" compress consecutive lines into ranges before hashing and prompting, or list every line? — check what `trace_entry` renders for `{"big.py": range(1, 50001)}`.
  - Context lines: a diff made without `--unified=0` makes `diff_hunks` count 3 context lines either side as "changed". That widens coverage and reachability. review-viewer uses `--unified=0`. Whether the review pipeline's diff does is unverified.
- **Concurrent or repeated use:**
  - **Generators.** `Iterable[int]` lets a caller pass a generator. D10 validates, D7 hashes, and coverage intersects, so the same values are walked at least three times. A generator is used up by the first pass, so later passes see no lines: the cache key has no ranges and nothing is covered. Unknown: whether `map_paths` turns each value into a list or set once at the start — pass `{"a.py": (i for i in [3])}` and check `changed_lines_covered`.
  - **Order.** Order does not matter, because D7 sorts before hashing.
- **Offline / unavailable / unauthenticated:** this does not apply to the mapping itself, since nothing is fetched. The producer needs a local `git diff base head`. The review pipeline gets that from the snapshot, with no network involved. The risk is a different one:
  - In a **multi-repo snapshot**, `git diff` paths are relative to each repo, but `changed_lines` keys must be relative to the snapshot (D2's `root`).
  - If the caller forgets to add the repo-directory prefix, no key matches an entry file. Every entry is dropped as `unreachable` or `no_changed_line_covered`.
  - No error is raised, and the run gives the same output as a run on a diff with nothing in it.

### Assumptions we are making
- No package named `changed-lines` is imported or installed by this change. `uv.lock` after the change gains `jsonschema` and nothing named `changed-lines` or `changed_lines`.
- Every `changed_lines` key the PR 2–4 callers pass is a snapshot-relative POSIX path with no `a/`, `b/` or other diff prefix and no surrounding quotes.
- Every line number is a head-side line, never a base-side one. A deleted line can never appear, so a deletion-only change is never in scope.
- The caller's diff uses `--unified=0`, so context lines are not counted as changed.
- `map_paths` reads each `Iterable[int]` exactly once and turns it into a list or set, so generators work.
- `map_paths` rejects a `str` or `bool` line value with `ValueError` before any `CallFn` call.
- The cache keys and prompts store changed lines as compressed ranges, so a 50k-line rewrite gives a prompt under a few KB.

### How we would find out cheaply
1. **No such package.**
   - Run `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://pypi.org/pypi/changed-lines/json`. A 404 confirms the package does not exist; a 200 would mean a name collision to investigate.
   - After the change, run `grep -i 'changed.lines' uv.lock`. Any match falsifies the first assumption.
2. **Producer quirks.** Run this from `skills/review/scripts`:
   ```bash
   python -I -c 'from review_pipeline.checks import diff_hunks as d; print(d("--- a/x.py\n+++ b/x.py\n@@ -5,2 +4,0 @@\n-a\n-b\n+++ \"b/my file.py\"\n@@ -1 +1 @@\n-o\n+n\n"))'
   ```
   - The deletion-only claim is falsified if `x.py` appears in the output.
   - The quoting claim is falsified if the key is the clean `my file.py`.
3. **Prefix and context config.** In the review fixture repo, run `git -c diff.mnemonicPrefix=true diff HEAD~1 | head -3`. Then check whether the pipeline's diff call passes `--unified=0` / `-U0`. If it passes neither, the context-lines assumption is false.
4. **Consumer behaviour.** Once `map_paths` exists, call it with a `FakeCall` three times:
   - `changed_lines={"a.py": (i for i in [3])}`: a covered line 3 confirms generators work, and an empty `changed_lines_covered` falsifies it.
   - `{"a.py": "12"}`: the `str` assumption is falsified unless this raises `ValueError` with `FakeCall.calls == 0`.
   - `{"big.py": range(1, 50001)}`: the compressed-ranges assumption is falsified if `len(FakeCall.prompts[0]) > 10_000`.
5. **Multi-repo prefix.** Use the multi-repo fixture and pass repo-relative keys, with no top-level directory. If `paths` comes back empty and nothing is raised, that confirms the silent failure. The cheap guard is to warn or raise when no `changed_lines` key matches any file in the snapshot.

## changed-lines-covered

### What it is
`changed-lines-covered` is not a third-party package. PyPI (`https://pypi.org/pypi/changed-lines-covered/json`) and npm (`https://registry.npmjs.org/changed-lines-covered`) both return HTTP 404 for that name, and no file in the working tree mentions `changed_lines_covered` or `changed-lines-covered`. The dependency scanner picked it up from design.md § D10, where `changed_lines_covered` is a field on each traced path in `paths.json`. The design defines it as "the sorted, de-duplicated set" of changed lines that fall inside the path's retained hops. This change writes and owns it. Nobody outside the project maintains it. It has two jobs:
- It decides which traced paths survive. A path that covers no changed line is dropped at stage `no_changed_line`.
- It is the first ordering key (`-len(covered)`) and so decides which paths fit under `cap`.

Nothing needs to be added to `pyproject.toml`. The real risk is that we define this field badly, not that someone else's library behaves unexpectedly.

### The contract we rely on
There is no external API. The internal contract comes from design.md and is quoted here verbatim, because the implementation and tests will be checked against it.

- Input, from the `map_paths` signature (D2):
  `changed_lines: Mapping[str, Iterable[int]] | None = None,`
- Validation (D10): "changed-line paths are normalised to POSIX with no leading `./`; absolute paths or paths escaping `root` raise `ValueError`; lines below 1 raise `ValueError` … A missing file is tolerated." All of this happens "before any `CallFn` call".
- Definition (D10): "A traced path covers a changed line when: the hop is one of the retained hops, so hops after a cut never count; and the hop's file equals the changed file; and the line falls in `[line_start, line_end]`. `changed_lines_covered` is the sorted, de-duplicated set. A path with no coverage is dropped at stage `no_changed_line` with reason `no_changed_line_covered`."
- Ordering (D10): `-len(covered)`, then retained hop count, then `KIND_RANK`, then path, then line. When scoped, paths past `cap` are dropped as `over_cap`.
- Cache key (D7): includes "sorted changed ranges", so a different `changed_lines` produces different trace keys.
- Output (D13): emitted inside `Path` objects that are validated by the generated `paths.v1.schema.json` (`_Strict`, `extra="forbid"`) before `write_paths_file` writes anything.

### Edge cases & failure modes
None of this has been observed, because the code does not exist yet. Each bullet gives the behavior the design specifies, or names the gap where the design says nothing.

- **Empty or degenerate input.**
  - `changed_lines=None` means unscoped. The design records "no scope drops" and `cap: null`, but never says whether `changed_lines_covered` is then `[]`, `null` or left out. Unknown: what does an unscoped path carry in this field? Check by reading the generated schema for `Path.changed_lines_covered` (nullable or not).
  - `changed_lines={}` skips the fallback (`empty_scope`), and every path is then dropped as `no_changed_line_covered`. The result is a valid but empty `paths` list, not an error.
  - `changed_lines={"a.py": []}` is a non-empty dict that holds no lines. The design's `empty_scope` test only matches `== {}`, so the fallback and all traces still run and spend model calls, and then every path is dropped. That is the costly surprise here: a scope with no lines in it still burns a full run.
- **Malformed or unexpected-format input.**
  - `Iterable[int]` accepts a generator. If the code iterates once for validation and again for coverage, the second pass sees nothing. Every path is then dropped as `no_changed_line_covered` with no error raised, which looks just like "the change touches no entry". This is the most likely silent failure.
  - `True` is an `int` in Python and passes the `>= 1` check as line 1. `"12"`, `12.0` and `None` are not covered by the stated validation. Unknown: are non-int lines rejected or coerced? Check with `map_paths(changed_lines={"a.py": ["12"]}, ...)` and expect `ValueError`.
  - Coverage compares the hop's file to the changed file with plain string equality. Changed paths are normalised (POSIX, no leading `./`). D9 rule 1 only checks hop paths for escaping `root`; it does not say they are rewritten. A hop citing `./pkg/a.py` or `pkg//a.py` would pass the gate and never match `pkg/a.py`.
  - Only the head side counts, because the gate rejects `base_side_citation`. A change made only of deletions has no head lines, so it cannot be covered, and every path is dropped.
  - A hop with `line_end < line_start` would cover nothing. The design does not say whether `Hop` validation rejects this. Lines past EOF in `changed_lines` are accepted (missing files are tolerated) and simply never match.
- **Oversized input.**
  - A newly added 50k-line file, passed as 50k individual ints, gives a `changed_lines_covered` list of up to 50k ints per path. That list is serialised with `indent=2` (one int per line) and schema-validated on every write. There is no truncation or limit in the design.
  - The cache key holds "sorted changed ranges", so the key stays small only if the ints really are compressed into ranges first. Unknown: is the list collapsed into ranges before it goes into the key and the `trace_entry` prompt? Check by logging prompt length for a 50k-line input.
- **Concurrent or repeated use.**
  - Coverage is computed after all traces finish, from stored answers in canonical order (D7), so trace completion order should not change it.
  - Changing `changed_lines` between runs changes every trace key. A "resume" that also widens the diff re-asks everything.
  - Reordered or duplicated line ints should hash the same, because inputs are sorted. That only holds if they are also de-duplicated before hashing, and the design says "sorted" but not "de-duplicated" for the key.
- **Offline / unavailable / unauthenticated.**
  - The calculation itself is pure in-process set arithmetic, with no network, git or model call.
  - It depends on retained hops, which need `resolve` + `git show` (gate rules 2–4). If git is missing or a sha is not reachable, hops break at rule 2. Paths then shrink or are dropped, and coverage falls with no error naming the real cause.
  - If `CallFn` fails with a recoverable error, the entry is dropped at stage `trace` before coverage is ever computed.

### Assumptions we are making
- No external package called `changed-lines-covered` is needed. The PyPI JSON API and the npm registry both return 404 for the name, and the post-change `pyproject.toml` adds only `jsonschema>=4`.
- `changed_lines` is materialised once (for example `{path: sorted(set(lines))}`) during validation. A generator input then gives the same coverage as the equivalent list.
- Hop file paths are normalised exactly like changed-line keys before comparison. A hop citing `./a.py` covers changed lines in `a.py`.
- Hops after a cut never add to coverage. If hop 3 breaks and hop 3 cites a changed line, that line does not appear in the field.
- `changed_lines_covered` is strictly increasing, with no duplicates, for every written path, and the schema enforces at least the int-ness and `>= 1`.
- The same `changed_lines` given as a list, a reversed list, a list with duplicates, or a generator produces identical trace cache keys and byte-identical `paths.json`.
- Non-int line values (`"12"`, `12.0`) raise `ValueError` before any `CallFn` call, and `True` is rejected rather than read as line 1.
- `changed_lines={"a.py": []}` is either treated as `empty_scope` or accepted on purpose. Either way, the behavior is pinned by a test, not left to chance.

### How we would find out cheaply
1. **Confirm it is not a package (already done; re-run in CI if wanted).**
   ```bash
   curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' https://pypi.org/pypi/changed-lines-covered/json   # 404 = not a package
   grep -n 'changed' plugins/multiplai-dev/lib/code_facts/pyproject.toml                       # must print nothing
   ```
   Any 200, or any match, falsifies the first assumption.

2. **Pin the semantics with a pure helper test.** Pull the D10 rule out as `covered_lines(retained_hops, changed) -> list[int]` and run five asserts:
   ```python
   ch = normalise_changed({"pkg/a.py": (n for n in [12, 12, 5])}, root)            # generator + dup
   assert ch == {"pkg/a.py": [5, 12]}                                                # fails → materialise/dedupe assumption wrong
   assert covered_lines([hop("./pkg/a.py", 10, 13)], ch) == [12]                     # [] → path-normalisation assumption wrong
   assert covered_lines(gate_retained(hops_broken_at_3_citing_line_5), ch) == []     # [5] → cut-hop assumption wrong
   for bad in (["12"], [12.0], [True], [0]): pytest.raises(ValueError, normalise_changed, {"pkg/a.py": bad}, root)
   ```

3. **End-to-end determinism with the `FakeCall` stub.** Run `map_paths` three times on one fixture, passing `changed_lines` as a list, as a reversed list with duplicates, and as a generator. Then assert:
   - `FakeCall` saw the same set of prompt keys all three times;
   - `write_paths_file` output is byte-identical;
   - `FakeCall.count == 0` on runs 2 and 3 with a shared `cache_dir`.

   Different bytes or extra calls falsify the cache and normalisation assumptions.

4. **Empty-lines scope.** Call `map_paths(changed_lines={"a.py": []}, ...)` and assert `FakeCall.count == 0` and `fallback.reason == "empty_scope"`, or whichever behavior the team chooses. A non-zero count means the scope with no lines still spends model calls.

Now the underlying `check_quote`.## citation-unverified

### What it is
`citation-unverified` is not a third-party package. The dependency scanner picked up a drop-reason code that design.md § D5 and § D11 define. I searched the repository for `citation_unverified|citation-unverified` and found nothing, so this change introduces the string. It is one value of the closed `DropRecord.reason` enum under stage `model_fallback_citation`. It is recorded when a model-fallback entry's citation has an absolute path, a `..` segment, a path `resolve` cannot place, or fails the re-read through `code_facts.check_citation`. The behavior behind the label is in-house code. `code_facts.explore.check_citation` is part of this repo's multiplai-dev plugin. It calls `multiplai_core.citations.check_quote`, an internal package that uses only the standard library and shells out to `git show`. The rest of this section describes how that existing code really behaves, because that decides which fallback entries get this label and which survive. Nothing needs adding to `pyproject.toml`.

### The contract we rely on
From `plugins/multiplai-dev/lib/code_facts/code_facts/explore.py`:

```python
Resolve = Callable[[str, Side], "tuple[str, str, str] | None"]
UNRESOLVED = "path names no known repo"

def check_citation(citation: Citation, resolve: Resolve) -> str | None:
    """None when the quote is inside the cited lines at its commit, else the reason it fails."""
    found = resolve(citation.path, citation.side)
    if found is None:
        # An empty quote is named first, whatever the path.
        return "empty quote" if not normalise_ws(citation.quote) else UNRESOLVED
    repo, sha, rel = found
    return check_quote(repo, sha, rel, citation.line_start, citation.line_end, citation.quote)

def ws_path(path: str, root: Path) -> str:
    """The path relative to the agents' working directory, for whatever form the agent wrote."""
```

From `multiplai_core/citations.py`:

```python
@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=2048)
def file_at(repo: str, sha: str, path: str) -> str | None:
    """... Results are cached per ``(repo, sha, path)``, so pass a commit sha, not a
    ref such as ``HEAD`` that can move. Bytes that are not UTF-8 are replaced."""

def lines_at(repo: str, sha: str, path: str, start: int, end: int) -> list[str] | None:
    """... An *end* past the end of the file returns the lines that exist. A range that is not valid
    (*start* below 1, or *end* before *start*) returns ``[]`` ..."""

def check_quote(repo: str, sha: str, path: str, start: int, end: int, quote: str) -> str | None:
    """None when *quote* is inside lines *start*..*end* of *path* at *sha*.
    Both sides are whitespace-normalised first ... On a failure it
    returns the reason: ``"empty quote"``, ``"path not at commit"`` or
    ``"quote not at cited lines"``."""
```

The citation model (`code_facts/models.py`) is `Citation(_Model)`. Its fields are `path: str`, `line_start: int = Field(ge=1)`, `line_end: int = Field(ge=1)`, `quote: str` (required), `id: str = ""` and `side: Literal["base","head"] = "head"`. An `after` validator raises when `line_end < line_start`. `_Model` uses `extra="ignore"`.

What the design adds on top: D5 step 2 rejects an absolute path or one containing `..` before calling `check_citation`. It collapses every non-`None` reason, plus `UNRESOLVED`, into the single literal `citation_unverified`.

### Edge cases & failure modes
- **Empty or degenerate quote.** `check_quote` returns `"empty quote"` for `""` or a quote that is only whitespace. This is checked before the path, so an empty quote on a path that does not resolve reports `"empty quote"`, not `UNRESOLVED`. Both become `citation_unverified`, and the difference is lost.
- **Degenerate quote that passes.** The match is a plain substring test on whitespace-normalised text (`wanted in normalise_ws("\n".join(lines))`). A one-character quote like `"("`, or a fragment that cuts through an identifier like `"rint("` for `print(`, is **verified**. A fallback agent can cite a line it never read and still pass, as long as a common token appears somewhere in the range.
- **Over-wide range.** `line_end` has no upper bound. `lines_at` slices `text.split("\n")[start-1:end]`, so `line_start=1, line_end=99999` returns the whole file, and almost any quote from the file passes. The "1-15 lines" in `citation_rules` is prompt text only and nothing enforces it. D5 step 5 (`duplicate`) compares only the cited line, so a whole-file citation is neither unverified nor a duplicate.
- **Range starting past EOF.** This gives an empty slice, so the result is `"quote not at cited lines"`, then `citation_unverified`. It does not raise.
- **Malformed range or missing quote fails the whole answer, not one entry.** `line_end < line_start`, `line_start: 0` or a missing `quote` key raises a pydantic `ValidationError` while `FallbackAnswer` is parsed. Under D5, that sets the whole fallback to status `failed`. Every other good entry in the same answer is lost, and none of them is recorded as `citation_unverified`.
- **Absolute paths are what the agent naturally writes.** The fallback agent runs with `cwd=root` and `Glob`/`Grep`, which return absolute paths. `ws_path` exists so that existing callers (`citation_keeper(..., root=...)`) strip the root prefix and `./` and accept such citations. D5 rejects absolute paths before any normalisation, so a correct citation like `/tmp/snap/repo/cli.py:12` is dropped as `citation_unverified`. Unknown: what share of real fallback answers use absolute paths. To check, run one fallback against a fixture and count the `path` values that start with `/`.
- **`..` and paths outside the repo inside `check_quote`.** D5 stops these before `git show`. If one got through, `git show <sha>:../x` exits non-zero, `file_at` returns `None`, and the reason is `"path not at commit"`, which is a reason string and not an exception.
- **`side="base"` in a fallback citation.** `Citation.side` accepts `"base"`. D9 has `base_side_citation` for trace hops, but D5 has no such rule. Whether a base-side fallback citation is verified, unresolved or raises depends on the caller's `resolve`. Unknown: what the prefix-splitting test resolver returns for `side="base"`. To check, call it with `("repo/x.py", "base")` and see.
- **Malformed file bytes.** `file_at` decodes with `errors="replace"`. A non-UTF-8 file does not fail; it matches against text that contains U+FFFD. A quote the agent copied from the same mangled view can pass.
- **Oversized file.** `git show` reads the whole blob into memory with `capture_output=True` and no `timeout`. A multi-MB generated file or a binary is read whole for every distinct `(repo, sha, path)`. For an LFS-tracked file, the quote is checked against the LFS pointer text.
- **Repeated use: stale cache.** `file_at` uses `lru_cache(maxsize=2048)` at process scope. `None` (file not found) is cached too. If `resolve` returns a ref such as `HEAD` instead of a sha, a later commit at the same repo path still gets the old text or the cached `None`. The docstring warns about this.
- **Concurrent use.** `check_quote` is a synchronous `subprocess.run` call. If it runs inside the async `map_paths`, every citation check blocks the event loop while other trace tasks wait. In CPython, `lru_cache` is safe to call from several threads, but two cold calls can both run `git show`. It does not corrupt state.
- **Offline or no git.** No network is involved. If the directory is not a git repo, or the sha is not in it, the call returns `"path not at commit"` and the entry becomes `citation_unverified`. A misconfigured `resolve` therefore looks like an agent error. If the `git` binary is not on `PATH`, `subprocess.run` raises `FileNotFoundError`. `check_citation` does not catch it, so it propagates out of `map_paths` as a fatal error and no drop record is written.
- **Reason detail is thrown away.** `check_quote` gives three different reason strings and `check_citation` adds `UNRESOLVED`. The closed enum has one value. Unknown: whether D11's `DropRecord` keeps the underlying reason anywhere (`detail`?). To check, look at the `DropRecord` model in `paths.py` once it is written. As specified, it has only `stage`, `entry` and `reason`.

### Assumptions we are making
- `check_citation` returns `None` only when the whitespace-normalised quote is a substring of lines `line_start..min(line_end, EOF)` at the resolved sha. Any other outcome is a non-`None` string, never an exception, as long as `git` is installed.
- Every non-`None` result from `check_citation` (`"empty quote"`, `"path not at commit"`, `"quote not at cited lines"`, `"path names no known repo"`) maps to `citation_unverified`, and no other drop reason.
- No real fallback citation will be absolute or contain `..`, so rejecting them before `ws_path` loses no correct entries.
- An invalid line range or a missing `quote` in one fallback entry is rare enough that failing the whole `FallbackAnswer` is acceptable. The alternative would be per-entry `citation_unverified`, which needs `citation: dict | None` plus validation per entry.
- The test resolver always returns a full 40-character sha, never `HEAD`, so the process-wide `file_at` cache cannot serve stale text across tests.
- `git` is on `PATH` wherever `map_paths` runs, including CI.
- Synchronous `git show` calls during fallback post-processing take little time compared with the model call. Fewer than about 50 citations per run, each well under 100 ms.

### How we would find out cheaply
Run one script from `plugins/multiplai-dev/lib/code_facts`:

```bash
uv run python - <<'EOF'
import os, subprocess, tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from multiplai_core.citations import check_quote, file_at
from code_facts import Citation, check_citation, ws_path
d = tempfile.mkdtemp(); g = lambda *a: subprocess.run(["git","-C",d,*a],check=True,capture_output=True)
g("init","-q"); Path(d,"m.py").write_text("def main():\n    print('hi')\n")
g("add","."); g("-c","user.name=t","-c","user.email=t@t","commit","-qm","x")
sha = subprocess.run(["git","-C",d,"rev-parse","HEAD"],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.strip()
for a in [("m.py",1,99999,"print"),("m.py",1,2,"rint("),("m.py",1,2,"main(): print"),
          ("m.py",50,60,"x"),("../m.py",1,1,"def"),("/m.py",1,1,"def"),("m.py",1,1,"  ")]:
    print(a, "->", check_quote(d, sha, *a))
print("ws_path:", ws_path(f"{d}/m.py", Path(d)))
for bad in [{"path":"m.py","line_start":3,"line_end":1,"quote":"x"},{"path":"m.py","line_start":1,"line_end":1}]:
    try: Citation.model_validate(bad); print("accepted", bad)
    except Exception as e: print("rejected", type(e).__name__)
print(check_citation(Citation(path="m.py",line_start=1,line_end=1,quote=""), lambda p,s: None))
file_at.cache_clear(); os.environ["PATH"] = "/nonexistent"
try: print(check_quote(d, sha, "m.py", 1, 1, "def"))
except Exception as e: print("no git ->", type(e).__name__)
EOF
```

What would falsify each assumption:
- **Strict substring match.** If row 1 (`1..99999`) or row 2 (`"rint("`) prints anything other than `None`, the matching is stricter than described here. If they print `None`, the bullets on over-wide ranges and degenerate quotes are confirmed.
- **Reason strings.** If row 4 prints anything other than `quote not at cited lines`, or rows 5 and 6 print anything other than `path not at commit` (or raise), the reason-to-`citation_unverified` mapping needs revisiting.
- **Absolute paths.** If `ws_path` prints `m.py`, then a correct absolute citation can be rescued, and D5's "absolute ⇒ `citation_unverified`" rule drops it for no reason.
- **Invalid range or missing quote.** If both `Citation.model_validate` cases print `rejected ValidationError`, a single bad entry fails the whole `FallbackAnswer`.
- **Empty quote.** If the empty-quote call prints anything other than `empty quote`, the ordering of reasons is different.
- **No git on PATH.** If the last line prints `no git -> FileNotFoundError`, then a missing `git` is fatal rather than a `citation_unverified` drop. That contradicts the "`git` is always present" safety net, and it decides whether `map_paths` should catch the error.
- **Absolute paths in practice.** Separately, run the D5 fallback once with the `FakeCall` replaced by the real `agent_call_structured` against one fixture. If any returned `citation.path` starts with `/`, the assumption that no real fallback citation is absolute is false.

I checked: `cli-argv` isn't a package. It's one of the matcher names in D12, and I looked at real tests in this repo to see how that matcher would behave on them. Writing the section now.

## cli-argv

### What it is
`cli-argv` isn't a third-party package. Nobody maintains it, there's no `cli-argv` on PyPI (closest names: `cli-args`, `argv`, `cliopts`), and there's nothing to install. The name comes from D12: `cli_argv` is one of the five kinds of match in the new `code_facts/e2e.py` static test listing. The dependency scan read that table cell as a library. (The scan is also off in a second way: it says "0 declared name(s)", but `lib/code_facts/pyproject.toml` declares `multiplai-core[sdk]` and `pydantic>=2`.) What the change really depends on is the CPython 3.12+ standard library `ast` module (`requires-python = ">=3.12"`), plus one assumption about how this repo's tests drive argparse CLIs. The matcher reads test files without running them. It looks for calls like `main(["render", "--repo", ...])` and links them to a discovered `argparse_subcommand` entry. That gives a test-to-entry-point link with nothing imported or run. This section describes that matcher, since it's code the team is about to write and rely on.

### The contract we rely on
- D12's rule, verbatim: `cli_argv` matches when the "callee resolves to the program's `main` or the function owning the subparser setup; first arg is a literal list or tuple of `str` constants containing the subcommand's name tokens, in order".
- Standard library calls used: `ast.parse(source, filename='<unknown>', mode='exec', *, type_comments=False, feature_version=None, optimize=-1)`. List and tuple literals come back as `ast.List` / `ast.Tuple`. String literals come back as `ast.Constant` with a `str` `.value`. f-strings come back as `ast.JoinedStr`, `*xs` as `ast.Starred`, and `str(x)` as `ast.Call`. In 3.12, null bytes raise `SyntaxError`, not `ValueError` as they did before 3.12. The Python docs warn: "It is possible to crash the Python interpreter with a sufficiently large/complex string due to stack depth limitations in Python's AST compiler."
- The argparse behaviour the matcher copies: `ArgumentParser.parse_args(args=None, namespace=None)`. When `args` is `None` it reads `sys.argv[1:]`. The subcommand token sits after any options that belong to the parent parser.
- How this repo writes these tests, as found in the code:
  - `pr_pipeline/__main__.py:70` has `def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:`, and `build_parser()` (line 22) owns `add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)`.
  - Tests call these forms: `cli.main(["render", "--repo", str(repo), "--change-dir", str(change)])` (`skills/pr/scripts/tests/test_commands.py:591`), `main(["--out", str(out), "review", "--repo", ...])` (`skills/review/scripts/tests/test_deps.py:251`), and `build_parser().parse_args(["open", ...])` (`test_commands.py:80`).

### Edge cases & failure modes
- **Literals that aren't all strings (the usual case here, not a rare one):** D12 asks for "a literal list or tuple of `str` constants". The repo's real CLI tests almost always mix in non-constant parts, for example `str(repo)`, `str(change)`, `str(tmp_path / "empty")` (`test_commands.py:591,605`; `test_promote_skill.py:229`; `test_epic_spend.py:109`). Read strictly, the rule matches **none** of these, and `cli_argv` comes back almost always empty with no error. To match, the code has to accept any list or tuple literal and compare only its `ast.Constant` str elements against the subcommand tokens.
- **Global options before the subcommand:** in `test_deps.py:251` the argv is `["--out", str(out), "review", ...]`. "Containing … in order" therefore has to be a subsequence check, not a prefix check. A subsequence check can then match too much: in `["build", "--change", "x", ...]` (`test_epic_spend.py:109`), any option *value* that happens to equal a subcommand name also counts as a token. The matcher doesn't know which options take values, so it can't tell the two apart.
- **Calls through a helper:** `test_commands.py:19` defines `run(argv)`, which calls `commands.run(build_parser().parse_args(argv))`, and `test_deps.py:251` hides `main([...])` inside a helper. Matchers only look at call nodes in the test body, and nested `def`s are skipped. Tests that go through these helpers get no `cli_argv` match, with no error and no skip record.
- **`build_parser().parse_args([...])`:** at `test_commands.py:80` the callee is the attribute `parse_args` on a call's result, not `main` or `build_parser` itself. D12's rule ("callee resolves to … the function owning the subparser setup") doesn't cover this unless the resolver is taught that `X().parse_args` counts as calling X.
- **Imports inside a function:** `test_commands.py:584` has `from pr_pipeline import __main__ as cli` inside the test function. If D12's "per-module import table" only reads module-level `Import`/`ImportFrom` nodes, `cli` won't resolve and the test isn't listed.
- **Empty or degenerate input:** an empty list `main([])`, or `main()` with no arguments. An empty token sequence is a subsequence of every list. For entries with no subcommand tokens (`main_module`, `project_script`), a naive check would match every `main(...)` call to that program. For `pr_pipeline`, `main([])` actually ends in `SystemExit(2)`, because the subparsers have `required=True`. Unknown: does `cli_argv` apply to entries without a subcommand at all? Check by asserting on a fixture that has `main([])` against a `main_module` entry.
- **Malformed input:** spliced or computed argv such as `[*BASE, "render"]`, `["render", *extra]`, `[f"{cmd}"]` or `ARGS + ["x"]` produces `Starred`, `JoinedStr` or `BinOp` nodes. None of these are "literal", so they don't match. Files that won't parse get `syntax_error`, and files that won't decode get `decode_error`. A source file with NUL bytes raises `SyntaxError` on 3.12, so it's recorded as `syntax_error`.
- **Oversized input:** `ast.parse` on very deeply nested expressions can raise `RecursionError` (or `MemoryError`), and D12 only handles `decode_error` / `syntax_error`. Such a file would crash `map_paths` instead of being skipped. There's no size limit or timeout anywhere in the design.
- **Concurrent or repeated use:** the matcher is a pure function of the parsed tree, the `pyindex` index and the entry list. `ast` keeps no global state, so running it again on the same snapshot gives the same output, and threads are safe. The real risk is in the shared parse cache (D4): if something mutates cached trees (for example, adding parent links), a second listing pass sees changed trees.
- **Offline / unavailable / unauthenticated:** none of this applies. It's standard library only, with no network access, no credentials, and nothing imported or run. Calls to `subprocess.Popen` / `os.system` would hit the D14 guard that makes them raise.

### Assumptions we are making
- Most of this repo's CLI tests pass argv as a list literal written directly in the test body. Wrong if more than half the `main(` / `parse_args(` call sites under `skills/*/scripts/tests/` go through helpers or computed lists.
- Only the str-constant elements need to be compared. Wrong if a strict "every element is a `str` constant" check gives zero matches on `test_commands.py:591`.
- Subcommand tokens can be found as an ordered subsequence without false matches. Wrong if any repo test has an option value equal to a sibling subcommand name and gets listed under the wrong entry.
- The program's `main` is always the callee. Wrong if `build_parser().parse_args([...])` (`test_commands.py:80`) or `cli.main` through a function-local import (`test_commands.py:584`) is left out of the listing for the `open` / `render` entries.
- `ast.parse` only fails with `SyntaxError` / `UnicodeDecodeError` on real repo files. Wrong if any file raises `RecursionError` or `ValueError`.
- An empty argv literal never links a test to a subcommand entry. Wrong if `main([])` is listed under `argparse_subcommand`.

### How we would find out cheaply
Run this five-line census from the repo root (`uv run python -I census.py plugins/multiplai-dev/skills`). It prints every argv-style call in the test files and says whether the strict D12 rule would accept it:

```python
import ast, sys, pathlib
for f in pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]).rglob("test_*.py"):
    for n in ast.walk(ast.parse(f.read_text())):
        if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and n.args and isinstance(n.args[0], (ast.List, ast.Tuple)) and ast.unparse(n.func).split(".")[-1] in ("main", "parse_args"):
            strict = all(isinstance(e, ast.Constant) and isinstance(e.value, str) for e in n.args[0].elts)
            print(f"{f}:{n.lineno} strict={strict} func={ast.unparse(n.func)} toks={[e.value for e in n.args[0].elts if isinstance(e, ast.Constant)]}")
```

What would prove each assumption wrong:
1. Mostly `strict=False` lines: the "str constants only" wording is unworkable and has to become "compare only the constant elements".
2. Lines where the first token starts with `--`: prefix matching is wrong, and a subsequence check is needed.
3. A `toks` list where an option value equals a sibling subcommand: subsequence matching gives false matches.
4. `func=build_parser().parse_args`: the callee rule has to cover `parse_args`.
5. Comparing the census count with `grep -c "main(\[" -r` shows how many calls sit in helpers that a test-body-only scan misses.

For the parse-failure assumption, run `python -I -c "import ast; ast.parse('('*1000+')'*1000)"`. If it raises something other than `SyntaxError` (for example, `RecursionError` or `MemoryError`), D12 needs a third skip reason.

Sources:
- [cli-args on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/cli-args) (closest real package name; not used here)
- [cli-args JSON on PyPI](https://pypi.org/pypi/cli-args/)

Nearly done: I've confirmed the Click and Typer `CliRunner` APIs, and found that the repo doesn't use either one. One last check on Typer's `invoke` signature, then I'll write the section.## cli-runner

### What it is
`cli-runner` is not a package, so nothing gets installed for it. The name comes from the `cli_runner` match kind in D12. That matcher recognises tests that drive a command through **`click.testing.CliRunner`**, maintained by Pallets as part of Click, or **`typer.testing.CliRunner`**, maintained by the FastAPI/Typer project. In this change, `e2e.py` reads test files with `ast` and looks for calls shaped like `<x>.invoke(<resolved group/app>, <literal args>)`. It never imports or runs `CliRunner`. The "dependency" is therefore a **source-code shape that our static matcher must recognise correctly**, not a runtime import. Nothing should be added to `pyproject.toml`. `code_facts` currently declares only `multiplai-core[sdk]` and `pydantic>=2`, and D13 adds `jsonschema>=4`. There is no PyPI project named exactly `cli-runner`. The nearest name is `clirunner`, an unrelated argparse-oriented fork, so adding something under that name would install the wrong package. A grep of the multiplai marketplace repo finds **no** `CliRunner`, `import click` or `import typer` anywhere. In this repository, the matcher only ever sees the test fixtures.

### The contract we rely on
We rely on the call shapes that the upstream APIs define. Signatures as documented:

- Click (stable docs, 8.4/8.5):
  - `click.testing.CliRunner(charset='utf-8', env=None, echo_stdin=False, catch_exceptions=True, capture='sys')`
  - `CliRunner.invoke(cli, args=None, input=None, env=None, catch_exceptions=None, color=False, **extra)`
  - `CliRunner.isolated_filesystem(temp_dir=None)`: deprecated in 8.5.0, "Will be removed in Click 9.0."
  - About `args`: "When given as string it will be interpreted as a Unix shell command. More details at shlex.split()."
  - About `catch_exceptions` on `invoke`: "If None, the value from CliRunner is used."
- Typer (`typer/testing.py`, master):
  - `def invoke(self, app, args=None, input=None, env=None, catch_exceptions=True, color=False, **extra) -> Result:`
  - Here the first argument is a `typer.Typer` instance, which `invoke` converts with `typer.main.get_command(app)`.
  - Since Typer 0.26.0, Typer **vendors Click** (`from ._click import ...`). `typer.testing.CliRunner` is Typer's own class, not a re-export of `click.testing.CliRunner`.
- pytest-click (third-party plugin): provides ready-made **fixtures named `cli_runner` and `isolated_cli_runner`**. Its kwargs are passed through to `click.testing.CliRunner(...)`.

What D12 needs from these:
- **Receiver:** `<x>` is a `CliRunner()` instance created from either import path.
- **Command:** the first argument resolves to one of these:
  - a `@click.group` / `@click.command` function;
  - a `typer.Typer()` assignment;
  - a sub-app added with `add_typer`.
- **Arguments:** the second argument (`args`) holds literal tokens that name the subcommand path.

### Edge cases & failure modes
- **Empty or degenerate input:** `runner.invoke(cli)` with no `args` is legal, and Click passes an empty argument list (`args or ()`). There are no tokens, so `cli_runner` as written ("literal args containing the subcommand's name tokens") can only match the group itself, never a subcommand. Unknown: should a no-args invoke count as e2e for the group entry, or for nothing? Check by adding a fixture test `runner.invoke(cli)` and deciding what the expected listing is. Unknown: the exit code for a bare group (usage plus 0 or 2) differs across Click versions. It doesn't affect static listing. Check with `python -c` against the installed Click.
- **Malformed or unexpected-format input: a string `args`:** Click documents that a string `args` is split with `shlex.split()`. `runner.invoke(cli, "sync --dry-run")` is therefore a real invocation of `sync`. D12 says "literal args" but doesn't say a `str` constant is split. If it isn't split, the matcher silently misses this common form.
- **Malformed input: the runner comes from a fixture.** The most common pytest idiom is `def runner(): return CliRunner()` in `conftest.py`, or pytest-click's `cli_runner` fixture. In both, the runner reaches the test as a **parameter**, not as a `CliRunner()` call or a local binding. D12's rule ("`CliRunner()` or a name bound to it") misses these unless fixture resolution, which D12 already does for patches, is also applied to the receiver.
- **Malformed input: command names don't match.** Click 8.2+ removes the suffixes `_command`, `_cmd`, `_group` and `_grp` when it derives a name from the function name, in addition to replacing `_` with `-`. This is my recollection of the 8.2.0 changelog; check it as below. For example, `def sync_cmd()` is invoked as `sync`. D4's "default names convert `_` to `-`" would name it `sync-cmd`, so a test calling `["sync"]` would fail to match. Typer derives names separately with its own rules.
- **Malformed input: options before the subcommand.** `runner.invoke(cli, ["--verbose", "sync"])` and `["--config", "x.toml", "sync"]` are both valid. A matcher that requires the name tokens "in order" as a prefix misses them. A matcher that just scans for the token can misread an option's value (`["--profile", "sync"]`) as the subcommand.
- **Malformed input: Typer apps.** With Typer, the first argument is a `Typer` object (`app = typer.Typer()`), not a decorated `def`. Resolving "group/app" has to follow an `Assign`, and for sub-apps the `name=` of `add_typer`. Tests sometimes pass `typer.main.get_command(app)` to `click.testing.CliRunner` instead. That is a call expression, not a name, so it won't resolve unless handled. Unknown: does `click.testing.CliRunner` accept a command from Typer's vendored Click (Typer ≥ 0.26)? Check with a two-line script in a venv with `typer>=0.26` and `click` both installed.
- **Malformed input: an invoke that runs but fails.** `catch_exceptions` defaults to on: `CliRunner(..., catch_exceptions=True)` in Click, and `True` directly on Typer's `invoke`. A test whose handler raises still "invokes" it, and the exception is swallowed into `result.exception`. A `cli_runner` match therefore shows that the test reaches the entry, not that the path ran successfully. The same holds when `input=None` and a prompt fires: it reads empty stdin and the command aborts instead of hanging.
- **Oversized input:** for us, this is static analysis only. Long literal lists cost nothing. Arguments built at runtime (`args=[*BASE, "sync"]`, `ARGS + [...]`, f-strings, `parametrize` values) are not literals, so they get **no match, with no diagnostic**. `CliRunner.invoke` itself has no timeout parameter, so running such tests is out of scope for this change.
- **Concurrent or repeated use:** Click documents that `CliRunner` "only works in single-threaded systems without any concurrency as it changes the global interpreter state". It swaps `sys.stdin`, `sys.stdout` and `sys.stderr`, and `isolated_filesystem` calls `os.chdir`. That doesn't hurt static listing. It would corrupt output if anyone later ran matched tests in-process inside `map_paths`'s `bounded(concurrency)` tasks. The matcher itself is pure and repeatable over the parse cache.
- **Offline / unavailable / unauthenticated:** nothing is fetched or imported, so whether Click or Typer is installed makes no difference. Our own repo has zero `CliRunner` usage, so in production on this repo `cli_runner` yields **zero matches**. An empty result looks the same as a broken matcher, and only fixtures can tell them apart. In a repo that has more than one Click major installed, the matcher can't tell which naming rules apply, because it doesn't read installed versions.

### Assumptions we are making
- No package named `cli-runner` (or `clirunner`) is needed, and `uv lock` after this change adds no `click`, `typer` or `pytest-click` to `code_facts`.
- Every `CliRunner` construction in target repos is imported from `click.testing` or `typer.testing`, by `from ... import CliRunner` or attribute access. No re-export through a project helper module hides it.
- Runner receivers are always a direct `CliRunner()` call or a local or module name bound to one. They are never a pytest fixture parameter. pytest-click's `cli_runner` fixture and `conftest.py` runner fixtures break this.
- `args` is always a list or tuple literal of `str` constants. A `str` literal never appears. Click documents that it is accepted and `shlex`-split.
- A subcommand's invoked name always equals the function name with `_` replaced by `-`. Under Click 8.2+, suffix stripping breaks this for `*_cmd`, `*_command`, `*_group` and `*_grp`.
- The subcommand tokens appear as a contiguous prefix of `args`, with no global options before them.
- A Typer app passed to `invoke` always resolves through a simple `Name = typer.Typer(...)` assignment in a module that the import table reaches.
- A test that matches `cli_runner` really runs the handler's code path. Because exceptions are caught by default, this can be false even when the test passes.

### How we would find out cheaply
1. **No new package needed:** run `grep -rn "CliRunner\|click\|typer" plugins/` in the multiplai repo, then `uv lock` and `git diff uv.lock` after the change. Any `click`, `typer` or `pytest-click` line in the diff falsifies assumption 1. Today's grep already returns nothing.
2. **Naming, string args, Typer resolution:** in a scratch venv with `uv pip install "click>=8.2" "typer>=0.26"`, run:
   ```python
   import click; from click.testing import CliRunner
   @click.group()
   def cli(): pass
   @cli.command()
   def sync_cmd(): click.echo("ran")
   print(list(cli.commands))                      # ['sync'] falsifies the "_ -> -" assumption
   print(CliRunner().invoke(cli, "sync").output)  # "ran" proves string args are shlex-split and used
   ```
   Add `import typer; from typer.testing import CliRunner as T; app = typer.Typer(); app.command()(lambda: None); print(T().invoke(app, []).exit_code)` to confirm that the Typer runner takes the `Typer` object. Then try `click.testing.CliRunner().invoke(typer.main.get_command(app), [])`: a non-zero exit code or an `AttributeError` in `result.exception` shows that vendored-Click commands don't cross runners.
3. **Matcher coverage:** add one fixture test file containing five tests:
   - `runner.invoke(cli, ["sync"])`
   - `runner.invoke(cli, "sync")`
   - a `runner` fixture parameter from `conftest.py`
   - pytest-click's `cli_runner` parameter
   - `runner.invoke(cli, ["--verbose", "sync"])`

   Run `list_e2e_tests` over it. Each test that is missing from `tests.e2e` falsifies the matching receiver, `args` or ordering assumption.
4. **Caught exceptions:** in the same fixture, make `sync` `raise RuntimeError` and assert that `CliRunner().invoke(cli, ["sync"]).exit_code == 1` with `result.exception` set. That shows a passing `cli_runner` test can hide a crashed handler, so the listing should not be read as "path verified".

Sources: [Click API docs (testing)](https://click.palletsprojects.com/en/stable/api/), [Typer testing tutorial](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/testing/), [Typer `testing.py` source](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fastapi/typer/master/typer/testing.py), [Typer: Vendored Click](https://typer.tiangolo.com/tutorial/click/), [Typer docs home](https://typer.tiangolo.com/), [pytest-click on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/pytest-click), [clirunner on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/clirunner)

## click

### What it is
Click is the Pallets project's library for building command-line interfaces out of decorators. You decorate functions with `@click.command` / `@click.group`, and Click builds `Command`/`Group` objects that parse argv and dispatch to subcommands. It is BSD-licensed and maintained by the Pallets team. The current release is **8.5.0 (2026-08-24)**, and 8.5.1 is listed as "Unreleased". Typer (fastapi/typer, by Sebastián Ramírez) sits on top of Click and generates Click commands from type hints. **This change never imports or installs click.** `entries.py` reads click and typer decorator shapes out of the snapshot's source with `ast` and turns them into `click_command` / `typer_command` entries (D4). `e2e.py` recognises `CliRunner().invoke(...)` calls in test files as the `cli_runner` match (D12). Click is "new to this project" only in the sense that our scanner now has to copy Click's and Typer's naming and dispatch rules exactly. It should **not** be added to `pyproject.toml`. What we depend on is Click's runtime behavior, which our static scanner has to reproduce without running anything.

### The contract we rely on
We never call this API. We copy what it does. These are the runtime rules the scanner has to match:
